components.text: Whether the rational case for determinism can survive Huemer’s appeal to reasons and intellectual appearances.
Whether the apparent obviousness of freely selecting among alternatives is trustworthy evidence.
Whether the apparent availability and control described by Huemer provide evidence that such freedom exists.
Whether advice, learning, and behavioral change remain intelligible if people lack freely available alternatives.
Whether rational or behavioral change requires an agent’s avoidable selection rather than causal alteration.
Whether advice, deliberation, and behavioral change make sense only if libertarian alternatives are available.
Whether reason-responsive change is impossible under deterministic causation.
Whether examples of pervasive biological and environmental influence establish exhaustive determination and eliminate alternatives.
Whether impaired or abnormal cases can establish the absence of freedom in ordinary unimpaired choices.
Whether the cited biological and environmental influences establish complete causal determination of ordinary choices.
Whether impairment cases justify the inference that no ordinary unimpaired decision leaves alternatives.
Whether historical intuitive errors defeat the justificatory role of present intellectual appearances concerning free will.
Whether the con argument can reject appearances without itself relying on logical and intellectual appearances.
Whether historical errors show that intellectual appearances cannot provide prima facie justification for free will.
Whether praise, blame, reward, and punishment must retain their free-will-based and retributive forms to remain intelligible.
Whether agent-controlled alternatives justify differential moral entitlement and retribution.
Whether practical dependence on praise, blame, punishment, and reward establishes their retributive moral justification.
Whether purely forward-looking deterrence can distinguish permissible punishment of an offender from framing an innocent person.
Whether purely forward-looking deterrence and incapacitation can justify punishing offenders without desert.
Whether a nonretributive account can explain why framing an innocent person is wrong while restraining an actual offender is permissible.
Whether subtracting blame and retribution predictably causes social collapse or can support humane practice.
Whether subtracting responsibility and retribution makes humane social practice incoherent or causes practical collapse.
Whether causal revision can preserve humane treatment without relying on retributive desert.
Whether the causal evidence shows only influence or instead justifies demanding an action independent of antecedent biological and environmental conditions.
Whether experienced freedom retains default authority as mechanistic causal knowledge expands.
Whether appearances of freedom retain sufficient warrant despite expanding mechanistic evidence about neural action.
Whether dependence on multiple antecedents establishes exhaustive determination rather than pervasive influence.
Whether incomplete scientific evidence should displace the prima facie appearance that one possesses free will.
Whether historical failures of intuition defeat the default epistemic status of present appearances.
Whether mechanistic dependence constitutes compelling evidence sufficient to defeat the appearance of free will.
Whether general historical unreliability removes the prima facie warrant of this appearance.
Whether scientific explanation requires deterministic causal closure rather than allowing indeterministic or reason-giving explanations.
Whether a complete explanation must exclude agent reasons that explain without determining the action.
Whether scientific explanation must be deterministic and therefore exclude reason-based, nondetermining explanations of choice.
Whether causal explanation requires complete independence from all prior conditions.
Whether a choice can be intelligibly explained without tracing the final selection to a further determining antecedent.
Whether a freely selected action can remain intelligible without a further determining cause of the final selection.
Whether every explanatory stopping point must instead be traced to antecedent neural conditions.
Whether explanation legitimately stops at an agent’s reasons or prior causes remain operative through the final selection.
Whether quantum indeterminacy can supply the agency missing from a nondetermined choice.
Whether the final selection can be an agent-controlled stopping point rather than the product of prior causes or randomness.
Whether quantum indeterminacy provides the relevant kind of freely authored agency.
Whether nondetermining reason explanations can preserve a philosophically significant form of controlled choice.
Whether any account of free will survives known biological and environmental influences.
Whether any philosophically significant conception of freedom survives known biological and environmental causation.
Whether nondetermining explanation preserves a meaningful form of agency.
Whether causally influenced reasoning can nevertheless constitute meaningful control over belief through weighing epistemic reasons.
Whether deliberative change is merely something that happens to a person rather than a controlled choice process.
Whether weighing reasons in belief formation can constitute control rather than merely mechanistic alteration by inputs.
Whether an agent-level deliberative process provides a philosophically significant form of control.
